remarks.after:
## Remarks

The naturality identity says that the following square commutes. The vertical maps are the canonical evaluation maps, and the lower map is the transpose of $T^*$.

```tikzcd
X \arrow[r, "T"] \arrow[d, "J_X" swap] & Y \arrow[d, "J_Y"] \\
X^{**} \arrow[r, "T^{**}" swap] & Y^{**}
```

Both paths from $X$ to $Y^{**}$ send $x$ to the functional $g\mapsto g(Tx)$ on $Y^*$, as computed in steps 1.1–2.1.

## Remarks

The naturality identity says that the following square commutes. The vertical maps are the canonical evaluation maps, and the lower map is the transpose of $T^*$.

```tikzcd
X \arrow[r, "T"] \arrow[d, "J_X" swap] & Y \arrow[d, "J_Y"] \\
X^{**} \arrow[r, "T^{**}" swap] & Y^{**}
```

Both paths from $X$ to $Y^{**}$ send $x$ to the functional $g\mapsto g(Tx)$ on $Y^*$, as computed in steps 1.1–2.1.

technique.before: **Proof technique:** For $1<p<\infty$, test the Radon-Nikodym density against bounded truncated extremizers and pass to the limit by monotone convergence. For $p=1$, level-set testing forces the essential supremum below the operator norm.
technique.after: **Proof technique:** For 1 < p < ∞, test the Radon-Nikodym density against bounded truncated extremizers and pass to the limit by monotone convergence. For p = 1, level-set testing forces the essential supremum below the operator norm.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The triangle illustrates the free extension of the product-indexed family. Write $u_{(i,j)}$ for the standard vector of $R^{(I\times J)}$, and let $\iota(i,j)=u_{(i,j)}$ and $b(i,j)=e_i\otimes f_j$. The diagonal is a set map; $\Phi$ is the module isomorphism of the statement.

```tikzcd
I\times J \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "b"'] & R^{(I\times J)} \arrow[d, "\Phi", "\cong"'] \\
& M\otimes_R N
```

The triangle commutes because $\Phi(u_{(i,j)})=e_i\otimes f_j$, as traced in proof step 3.1. More generally, for every finitely supported coefficient family $(c_{ij})_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$,

$$\Phi\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in I\times J}c_{ij}u_{(i,j)}\right)=\sum_{(i,j)\in I\times J}c_{ij}(e_i\otimes f_j).$$

These sums are finite even when $I$ and $J$ are infinite. If either index set is empty, the top-left set is empty and both module vertices are zero, as in step 3.2. The given bases suffice; no further choice of basis is involved. The proof above is independent of the illustration.
